David Tibet reawakens his landmark ’84 debut, proper, as Current 93; a primordial stew of tape loops, atonal electronics, blood curdle exhortations and altogether ill-willed heck on the A-side, countered by a flip of more sepulchral spatialisation and a bewitching Annie Anxiety that calves off into the abyss, all captured during a time when they lived in a squat and danced with Youth at goth crucible, The Batcave. Sacred stuff for anyone into NWW, earliest Coil / Zos Kia, Psychic TV...

"Current 93’s first and last album, NATURE UNVEILED dragged together my obsessions, as I had decided to make a pop album that dealt with my (then—as now!) primary fascinations: Christian apocalyptic and eschatological Christian texts. In my Speed-Ridden Soul and Mind, I thought I was reinventing The Ronettes, and that the 2 long sides of NATURE UNVEILED were A- and B- Sides of a Wall Of Soundhogs HIT! But the reality is that I was sharing a squat in Vauxhall with Little Annie Anxiety, and hanging out with Youth in The BatCave, with chickens rescued by The Animal Liberation Front in our backyard. Or did that come soon after, soon later? The album was recorded at The Roundhouse Studios in London’s Chalk Farm, home of Bronze Records, the label of my heroes (then—as now!) Uriah Heep, and Motörhead too, for whom I had moved stage-gear on their tour promoting their debut single on Chiswick Records. Anyway, anyway—I had not reinvented The Ronettes, though every time, every place, I listen to NATURE UNVEILED it Hits.

- David Tibet, Hastings, 11 March 2026."

items.body:
Indonesian instrument-builder and folk mutator Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi meets wildman Shigeru Ishihara (aka Scotch Rolex) on a 2nd Takkak Takkak screwball for Nyege Nyege Tapes, tipped FFO Gabber Modus Operandi, Hulubalang, Raja Kirik, Lord Spikeheart.

One up to the duo’s eponymous debut of 2024, the possessed tempest of ‘Abu’ opens wormhole portals to fantasy dimensions triangulated with frightening vibrancy. The 40 minute trip goes hard into sweltering zones where ancient folk rituals encounter modern technology and psyches, replete with shifting atmospheric conditions and febrile oneiric logic. The results are a hyperrealistic projection of heck, taking listeners by the scruff of the neck and plunging them into an anomalous sort of fantasy island or parallel world teeming with phosphorescent life, from the animalcule level to the metaphysical. 

The ceremonial atmosphere of opening track 'Hai no uta' mixes Javanese gong with flute blasts  interspersed with unsettling electronic vibrations, while the title track takes shape through hoarse chants and a cocktail of rhythms: tuned, gamelan-like resonances through ordered electro-plated taiko structures, evolving into fractured free improv and syrupy drone metal. The album keeps shifting through these tense ceremonial sounds and hard dance textures, inviting heavy electronic kicks into the mannered mass of flutes and metallophone, matching acoustic instrumentation with carnivalesque synths and hardstyle rhythms.

Get your imaginary jabs in: it’s wild out there.

Really feeling this trippy acid treat by a one-of-a-kind Lolina; her 10th solo album since the most last Hype Williams drop with Dean Blunt in the early 2010s, and typically riddled with low-key mischievous slants on mutant dance-pop, as heard in her regular midweek club night at ace London venue, Spanners

Chasing up to her trip-hop tinted LP ‘Unrecognisable’ (2024), and a mix CD as Balmainjeans repping her club night ‘Distressed’, Lolina plays to an ideally unpredictable form with a shift into acid pop on ‘Monopoly of Mistakes’; eleven concentrated formulations of dry drum machines x tweakiest 303 gunk gilded with those vocals that keep us coming back. The combo of silver box and slanted vox finds the DIY prism-pusher bending timelines thru lo-fi indie-pop with sound system steppas, basement noise, cold wave and free party acid tekno, but never quite settling into any one style.

Maintaining her mutable range of variations within a theme, Monopoly of Mistakes really catches our breath with the way Lolina turns a paucity of ingredients into a dead satisfying thing. Whether commanding the 303 to the beat-less abstraction ‘Border Beach’ or alloying with wooziest keys and steppas fizz on ‘The Mercenaries’, or going deep into the lushest wormhole on her titular, 7 minute standout, her min-to-max sense of economy is key to this LP’s appeal. It’s there in the piquant synth-pop of ‘Menace’ and ‘Everlasting’ - think Wee Papa Girl Rappers meets Dave Ball at John T. Gast’s - and calling to mind a lost SOPHIE x EVOL gem in ’Stand Off’. But it’s also finely measured with an utterly gorgeous new age miniature harking to classic Hype Williams on ‘Welcome to the Drift of Whats Already Begun’, and of course the zinging closer ‘Penalty’, where zippiest ‘80s french cold wave meets AFXian harmony in a chef’s kiss demo of the extended melodic wooo that sets all her work apart.

Best believe it’s fully distinctive, addictive gear.

A properly delectable suite of sexy, downbeat dream-pop returns on 3rd pressing with its maker, Kai Hugo’s Antwerp-based World of Paint, acutely tipped to those who missed the 2020 + 2021 editions, and anyone who holds a flame for Johnny Jewel, Julee Cruise, Dirty Beaches

Back by demand - 2nd hand copies are known to trade for triple figures - ‘I’m Cindy’ is a chef’s kiss of effortlessly slow, seductive lo-fi songwriting that practically smushes earlobes with its heavenly marriage of Kai Hugo, aka Palmbomen’s faded production lustre and singer, Blue LoLãn’s range of whispered sweet nothings and harmonised coo. In the years since its original release it’s taken on a life of its own as a go-to succour for lovers of blissed-out, cinematic waft with equal measures of soft-focus, nostalgic FM synth gauze and details that caress, crack in all the right, tender places. 

Conceptually derived from Palmbomen II’s ‘Memories of Cindy’ session of 2017, the 13 tracks find marbled whorls of sensual fascination within that LP’s fantasy reminiscence, here expanded into a spectrum of LA-via-Antwerp dream-pop like Johnny Jewel meets Alex Zhang Hungtai on the synth and sax pearl ‘Another’ or lip-smacking cruiser ‘Justin’, thru a Voice Actor-esque ‘Voice Message’ and the gossamer FM synth fronds that wrap it up on ‘Maybe Because It’s Over Now’, whilst secreting shimmers of Vince Clarke ballads in ‘2y & 6m’, and acid-laced lo-fi machine crack shades away from Maria Minerva on ’Never Let Me Go’.

No brainer!

‘Aftersun’ composer Coates furnishes a score of heart-in-mouth classical strings, keys and choral arrangements to gay romance flick ‘Pillion’, aka an opportunity to ogle Alexander Skarsgård, replete with biker leathers, in a sub-dom relationship

By now one of the preeminent composers in his field - up there with Mica Levi, 0PN, Bobby Krlic et al - Coates continues to expand and hone his distinctly classic yet fresh palette and chops to purpose on this particularly lush set of orchestrations and sweeping sound design, including his take on a Satie evergreen. Gently gelled to the film’s narrative, revolving a shy yung queer lad seduced into a BDSM relationship with a dashing local biker, Coates’ score is ravishingly sensual and heady, full of oneiric allusions to classical, ambient, lavish ballads and twinkling electronica, all sure to hit pleasure centres of anyone who fancies Romance, Jonny Greenwood’s ‘Phantom Thread’ OST, Enya’s crushed velvet wafters, or event schmaltziest ends of Leyland Kirby.

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
Real heart-stopping, life-affirming, almost indescribably beautiful posthumous album featuring (for the first time) vocal works by beloved, dearly departed, Ethiopian nun and now-legendary pianist/composer Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru, room recorded straight to tape between 1977-1985, sounds of life just about audible in the background. Almost had an out of body experience listening to it the other night - just a perfect, 10/10 album.

’Souvenirs’ is an intimate self-portrait written, recorded and compiled by the late Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru; a classically-trained pianist turned nun, whose singular style of jazz and blues-inflected composition and performance became globally renowned in her latter years via reissues and compilations reaching as far back as the 1960s, namely the ‘Éthiopiques 21: Piano Solo’ CD and a much-prized eponymous set in 2016. At the age of 99, Emahoy passed away in Jerusalem last year, whilst planning towards this first ever showcase of her vocals - which have never appeared on her purely piano-based recordings until now, making for a truly life-affirming experience from its opening bars. 

The posthumous release, realised in collaboration with Emahoy’s family and Mississippi Records - is a stone cold stunner. It grants unprecedented access to her discrete craft and inner world in Addis Ababa, against a backdrop of the Ethiopian Red Terror and Civil War, prior to her subsequent exile in a Jerusalem convent. Whilst all no doubt defined by her signature, intricate and lilting type of classical meets jazz-blues phrasing, the eight songs are all far more concise than her usual instrumental works, made even more spellbinding by the revelation of her softly contoured and captivating vocals that beautifully trace and overlie the cadence of her keys. It’s just pure, unbridled expression that’s only heightened by the seemingly off-the-cuff nature of the recordings, as if she just sung the songs to herself, impromptu, never intended for public consumption.

Replete with incidental creaks of the piano stool, birds outside the window, and Emahoy’s finger on the record button, the songs depict themes of loss, mourning and soon-to-be exile, sung into a basic boombox. They place us in the room with her, closer than ever, privy to a vocal version of the closing number to her eponymous compilation, now unveiled as a dedication her niece, the titular Tenkou, with lyrics to guide her adulthood “Don’t cry / Childhood won’t come back / Let it go with love”, alongside the beatific, open-window paean ‘Clouds Moving on the Sky’, and melancholic hiraeth of ‘Ethiopia My Homeland’ or ‘Don’t Forget Your Country’, and ineffable, humbling elegance of idea and execution to ‘Is It Sunny or Cloudy in the Land You Live?’ and ‘Where is the Highway of Thought?’.

Unmissable.

Dutch techno duo Artefakt invite KMRU to assist on their third 'Collaborations' volume, improvising with the Kenyan sound artist in the studio to capture the immediacy of their exchange.

'Collaborations III' follows last year's short, sharp EP with Mayaan Nidam and its predecessor, a record of deep techno variations made alongside Sardinian producer Claudio PRC. This one's the series' most generous set so far and started life in 2023 when the trio found themselves at Pulse, a wooden cabin-cum-studio in the Brandeburg forest. This is where most of the improvisations were initially formulated and in the second session, at Artefakt's Berlin studio, they dubbed the two solo piano tracks and finished the arrangements. It's charming material, as you might imagine, that deviates from Artefakt's prior material and KMRU's noisy recent gear. Made mostly of pillowy, synth-led drones and subtle environmental sounds, it's prime gear for sinking into your surroundings to.

items.body:
Effortlessly easy on the ear and yet still somehow fathoms-deep, Tara Clerkin Trio’s latest is their most refined and fully-formed transmission yet, mining a precious sweetspot between chamber-jazz, Plone-style bric-a-brac electronics, Crescent’s lo-fi reveries and the urban pressure of the Young Echo collective, unpicking decades of British musical history in the process. Trust, it’s a special one.

Like every great band, TCT know their history. They've grown up with and formed their identity in the shadow of Bristol's musical lore, whether it's The Pop Group, Massive Attack or Flying Saucer Attack, and when they use traceable elements, it feels like a believable part of their DNA. Thankfully, they meaningfully add to that narrative too, not adapting an aesthetic for easy consumption. Part of this might be down to their makeup; they formed in the late 20-teens from the ashes of the Tara Clerkin Band, a larger ensemble that Clerkin had put together to expand the scope of her folk-y pop compositions. And when most of the members moved on, stepbrothers Sunny-Joe Paradiso and Patrick Benjamin stuck around to see where the road might lead. All "proper" players, they've traditionally let their songs appear from what sounds like loose, casual improvisations, like you're tuned into Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society' band running through Laika's 'Silver Apples of the Moon'.

So you get a song like the brilliant 'Ups & Downs', that simmers for a good four minutes with wheezing harmonium, double bass and clarinet, percussion just rumbling in the background somewhere, before a jerky sampled beat, Mellotron strings and Clerkin's voice would have you thinking Matt Elliott's behind the boards. But 'Somewhere Good' is also remarkably tight when it needs to be, walking a tightrope between easy breezy and meticulous with acrobatic skill. Opener 'Lake Walk', for example, sounds intentionally naive, jammed out loosely on synthesised and real woodwind that's caught in a vortex of Space Echo, before 'Lazy Daisy' cuts it short with its more ordered (but still kinda slouchy) beat-heavy dreampop atmosphere. It's where the album's shape really coagulates, between Broadcast's dramatic early EPs (back when they were touring with Plone) and Pram's best shit, just lightly tweezed at the edges, its creases relaxed to fit in with Laila Sakini's quietly genius 'Paloma'. And that mood carries the record even when Clerkin's voice - pursed into a soulful croon or a lackadaisical murmur - vanishes completely. One of the most gripping moments arrives with 'There Was a Nice Sunset', effortlessly matching slowcore drums with piano flourishes and synths, locking into the same general feeling but widening the boundaries, nodding to Adrian Sherwood's lysergic work on Creation Rebel's 'Starship Africa'. 

There's years of British musical history baked into this stuff, and yet it feels wholly new.

Re-mastered edition of Vini Reilly’s gorgeous 1996 side of burbling synth-pop and electro-dub, freshly reshuffled from the 2007 CD and expanded with a rare 1992 cut, ‘The New Fidelity’

Vini Reilly’s The Durutti Column had, by 1996, exerted a lot of influence on the post-punk, synth/indie-pop and early acid house/balearic scene, and by the mid ‘90s their music leaned into what was by then called “chill out”. Now expanded to 12 songs, their ‘Fidelity’ album stills glows with an after-party or early morning phosphorescence, drifting between sleek and crunchy machine rhythms while Vini and Eley Rudge alternate husky, opiated, and sweetly prim dreampop vocals, all wrapped in TDC’s signature, ribboning synth and guitar melodies.

Where the original album shored up at the Fleetwood Mac-meets-Jackie Mittoo stylings of ‘Guitar For Mother’, this first, definitive vinyl pressing bleeds out into two bonus songs. Taken from a Total Guitar covermount CD in 1995, ‘My Only Love’ is a beautifully strung out shadowplay of reverberatign guitar and echoic vox in mouth-watering style, while ’The New Fidelity’ is a spiralling nod to Vini’s krautrock/kosmiche and flamenco influences swept up in plonging FX that sweetly see off the record. Added to absolute gems such as the saddlesore trip-hop/folk of ‘Fidelity’, the balearic blues of ‘Future Perfect’ and the light-headed synth-pop of ‘Abstract of Expression’, you’ve got a real pearl.

Late, great Finnish maverick Mika Vainio’s debut ’94 minimal techno masterpiece, originally conceived as Ø, is treated to a much needed reissue, newly expanded with all tracks from the CD on vinyl for the first time and including the absolute all-timer ‘Lasi’ - 100% unmissable if you know what’s good.

Back in circulation 20 years square since the 1st vinyl edition, and just over 30 years since the CD, ‘Metri’ serves a stone cold but heart-melting reminder of Mika’s way with puristic electronics. All 15 tracks from the CD are now cut to vinyl for a definitive edition of Mika’s exemplary solo statement, which would arrive the same year as his debut with Pan Sonic (the ‘Panasonic’ EP). It would dovetail with a time when the original Chicago, NYC and Detroit house and techno templates were being morphed in translation by new waves of artists such as Mika and his pal Ilpo Väisänen, or the likes of Richie Hawtin or Dan Bell, who all effectively streamlined the tekkerz of DJ Pierre, Blake Baxter and Rob Hood to even more stringent levels. 

What distinguishes Mika’s debut as Ø from all of the above is his feel for frosted tone and edge-of-distortion bite, rendered wth resounding plangency; all perhaps stereotypically reflective of his subarctic climes and expressing a sonic personality that would come to define certain strands of electronic music for decades to come, before his untimely passing in 2017, and ever since. We’ve lost count of the times the breathtaking motif of ‘Lasi’ has prompted us to a heads-down, air-punching jack, and reduced rooms at the afters to wide-eyed silent awe, until someone has to ask for an ID. 

Along with the likes of body-bouncing pulse and mind-bending acid tone to ‘Kuvio’ and ‘Twin Bleebs’, the uncanny amniotic ambience of ‘Radio’ and border-watch ambient tension of ‘Kenttä’, or the prototypes for his pure noise works in the ‘JL-CSG’, thru the sublime tension of ‘Dayak’, it’s every bit the ultra classique and we envy anyone coming across this album for the first time. Like many others, we will be taking the opportunity to replace well worn copies with a freshie to rinse and repeat for decades to come.

Seriously this one’s going to the grave with us.

items.body:
Gary Sullivan, host of WFMU's Bodega Pop, pools his Brooklyn and Queens finds on this crunchy anthology, collecting early 20th century Russian music that was prized by first-generation Russian New Yorkers.

Time's frozen on 'Let Me Perish Without Return', a set of noisy ballads, music hall standards and folky reflections that map out the experience of the diaspora who immigrated from the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union as the home they knew transformed beyond recognition. Sullivan combed thrift stores in Forest Hills, Brighton Beach and Gravesend to find these intriguing cues, and pieces together a story that's shared by half a million New Yorkers. The remnants of Russian life are still visible on the surface of these neighborhoods, and the music helps us understand the culture a little more deeply. It's not particularly familiar material, but it makes for fascinating listening - especially if you've rinsed the rest of the Death is Not the End catalog.

After a few trips ‘Around the Sun’ Mr Fingers returns to the ‘floor with a definitively broad selection of deep house and acid aces betraying the sound’s links with soul jazz as much as Italo disco and ambient synth musics.

‘Leev Ur Mynd’ is the prescriptive title of Larry Heard’s 7th studio LP in his OG mode, which lands just over 40 years since his early 12”s initiated a sea-change in club music. On a dozen cuts the veteran effortlessly ushers debonaire dancefloors to his command, from proper ChItalo acid peacockery in ‘Plastic Nightmares’ to the piquant electro-soul flow of ‘Replicate’, and covering the finest spectrum of styles & patterns within a theme in between. 

His influential mastery of the 303 results in thee juiciest acid on the LP title tune, then tweaked to a charming type of bloozy jig in ‘Barndance’, and woven into the album’s tuffest jam ‘Menagerie’, or more subtly riding the piano-led glyde of ‘April Rain’, whereas the rest tends towards his equal bias for slicker soul-jazz and Afro-Latinate slink. Deeper lounge lizards will get theirs in the syncopated shimmy of ‘The Happening Thing’ and the sublime vocal chops of ‘When You Need Me’ and ‘All I Need’, thru the frankly sexy ‘Tension’ and that chef’s kiss twinkle of percussion and choral pads in ‘Ribbons.’

What a G?! Tip!

items.body:
UK born, Shanghai-based producer SHALT presents Votive via Infinite Machine.

"SHALT lands on Infinite Machine for a full-length. The album is entitled Votive, functioning as an exploration of memory and how, "over time, recollections of words and meanings become hazy and decayed, in turn taking on new forms and purposes

Votive comes from a sense of an offering in 'devotion to a memory'. The offering that Votive makes is an overt one, where very little is held back. In this spirit, the album wears emotion on its sleeve: the grooves, the chords, the melodies are big and immediate, especially at the front end of the album. As it progresses and over the second half it draws in on itself, becoming more reflexive but no less sentimental, and a poignant melody or atmosphere is never far at hand.

Mangled vocals appear and then recede throughout the proceedings. You’d be mistaken, however, if you thought this provides immediate humanity: the processing and the unintelligible words keep the warmth at arms’ length, as if dealing with ghosts. According to SHALT himself, “words are removed from their original context, given different meaning by recasting the voice into new elements, rather than relying on the original language itself”. Indeed, often, a voice can only barely be made out as such, morphed beyond recognition into a lead synth or an alien texture.

Overall, Votive is more cinematic and expansive than any of SHALT’s previous releases, as if the familiar traits and gestures (big square-wave basslines, 3-D IMAX leads) were given free rein and were finally allowed to stretch out to their full potential, freed from the constraints of the dancefloor."

‘Aste’ was first issued in 2006, but derives from a pivotal era 1992-1993, following years of Mika throwing raves between Finland and Russia with the Hyperdelic House crew, where they mostly played imported 12”s picked up during trips to Berlin or London. Mika would effectively make his own tunes inspired by those 12”s, generating a string of foundational EPs (‘Röntgen’ & ‘Kvantti’) and the landmark album ‘Metri’, along with this pack of weird but deadly effective box bangers. Now on their 2nd wind, it’s not hard to hear the inspiration of Chi, Detroit and NYC on this phase of Mika’s music, which would never be properly reprised quite this way, but surely endured as the clearest prompt for minimal techno productions by Richie Hawtin or Roger Semsroth’s Sleeparchive over the subsequent decade.

Between the relatively straight played Detroit electro-techno pulse of ’Spiraalit’ and waltzing icicles of ‘Siimes’ Mika yokes his machines to a singular aesthetic, firming up a style of hands-on, shapeshifting  techno craft that would be often imitated but rarely bettered. Hallmarks of sounds to come are gauged in the deliquescent bass and ringing pulses of ’Sukeltava’, the bone-dry 909 clack of ‘Pakkasherra’, and with hints of his dare-to-differ approach on the warped ambient collage that gives way to fierce warehouse propulsion on ‘Kolmas’. Seeds of his steely bangers from 1994 as Panasonic with Ilpo Väisänen are felt in the hypnotic pulse of ‘Aaltovaihe’, and likewise for his increasingly spaced out Ø works that would result in his recent, posthumous, final album in the sublime weightless drift to ‘Maan Valossa’.

Alt Dub label head Federsen links with Belgrade’s Estray for a deep, percussive exploration of dub house.

"A key figure within Eastern Europe’s electronic landscape, Estray has spent over a decade shaping a sound that travels far beyond his home base. With releases on Rebellion, Neptune Discs, Sol Selectas, Akumandra and Buddha Bar, alongside an extensive international DJ presence, his output reflects a balance of cultural depth and dancefloor functionality.

His productions draw on a wide palette of influences, fusing African and Latin rhythmic structures with rolling, dub-informed low-end. Intricate drum programming and fluid groove design sit at the core, while his basslines—heavy, warm and propulsive—remain a defining signature. Federsen, known for releases on Echospace Detroit, Grayscale, Synchrophone, Lempuyang and Avant Roots, continues to refine a sound rooted in analogue process, spatial detail and textural precision. His work leans into restraint, allowing depth and subtle modulation to drive momentum.

Recorded at Devon Analogue Studios, the pair’s collaboration unfolds across four tracks built on dense sub frequencies, shifting percussion and evolving atmospheres. Each piece is carefully structured yet organic, moving between stripped-back dub frameworks and more rhythmically charged passages.

The result is a cohesive body of work that sits comfortably within the dub house tradition while introducing a broader, multicultural rhythmic language—equally suited to immersive listening and deep dancefloor moments."

items.body:
Debut LP of dusty Americana and psych folk songs by members of Jow Jow & Sunburned Hand of the Man, plus the likes of Gary war and Wednesday Knudsen, all steeped in tradition and ‘60s revival styles of Fairport Convention, Pentangle, Anne Briggs, Linda Perhacs.

"Given the pair’s respective roots—and the presence of collaborators drawn from across the Northeast experimental underground—one might expect “a brutal blast of acid swirl.” Instead, what emerges is something far more unexpected. The album is “steeped, not in noise and dissonance, but in the fragrant, captivating folk of Linda Perhacs, Judee Sill, Karen Dalton, and Bridget St John.”

From the opening moments, especially on “Rosa,” the record reveals its core sensibility: “a ballad that digs deep into the psychedelic-folk tradition until it takes root in a freshly sporous permaculture.” What follows is a set of songs that feel both carefully assembled and organically grown—delicate structures held together by a wide circle of contributing musicians, including Wednesday Knudsen (flute), P.G. Six (harp, guitars, keys), Gary War (synth), Jen Gellineau (viola, violin), Willie Lane, L. Gray, and others.

Rather than functioning as studio additions, these collaborators form a genuine collective presence. “The family affair feeds into the album’s charms,” and the feeling is unmistakably communal. Like many of the ‘60s folk records it echoes, Stella Kola carries “the feeling of community and camaraderie” at its core, shaping a warmth that runs through the entire release.

The album’s emotional palette leans toward a quiet, persistent melancholy: “the best records from that era also carried with them an inherent sadness and Stella Kola’s songs wash over the listener with a beautiful woe.” Its sound edges into the terrain of Fairport Convention and Pentangle, with references to “Beggar’s, Kings, Dark Damsels, and Tarot,” yet never settles into revivalism. Instead, Ketch and Thomas extend the tradition outward, refracting it through their own distinctly American, underground language."

items.body:
C93’s second album, following ‘Nature Unveiled’ (1984) in the same year, continued to break new ground in the post-industrial arena with problematic visionary David Tibet leading a phalanx of co-conspirators - Steven Stapleton, Diana Rigerson, Steve Ignorant (Crass), among them - into fractious, psychoacoustic heck starkly contrasting his later neofolk works. Required listening FFO Gen P-O/TG/Psychic TV, NWW, Coil.

"Reeling In The Weeks—which felt like Years — after my first Current 93 album, I had started on the difficult second C93 album, DOGS BLOOD RISING.Having been asked to appear on both Top Of The Pops AND The Old Grey Whistle Test 93 times in the same week after the release of NATURE UNVEILED, I realised that God was telling me that I had hit on a winning formula of Christian eschatology and Apocalyptic Christian texts over a SoundScape As Cool As Flies, but that I was missing the vital ingredient of a Simon & Garfunkel song. DOGS BLOOD RISING — which I described to myself in a VISION as an album which hoped, wished, and made bad trips sound like good trips — was essentially the Mirror Night of NATURE UNVEILED, although only half of it was recorded at Roundhouse Studios. Squats were calling, and 8-track studios were all I was able to afford. DOGS BLOOD RISING didn’t chart, except in my NightSweats. Listening to it now, it makes me as restless as I was then, staring beyond the windows there, watching and praying for something, someone, anything, anyone.

- David Tibet, Hastings, 11 March 2026."

items.body:
Nearly three decades since it was created, The Durutti Column's "lost" fourth album is finally issued - with Factory Benelux catalogue number 36, and all.

According to legend, the original album was scheduled for release on Factory's Belgian subsidiary but an executive decision from Tony Wilson shelved it in favour of 1984's 'Without Mercy'. Darla Records have picked up the thread in reverent fashion, commissioning a prime remaster, and new artwork from Crepuscule designer Benoit Henneber.

Some tracks have appeared on Crepuscule's beautifully curated compilations over the years, but ultimately this is a real missing gem from the early Factory era: those skeletal drums, the sparse daubs of synth and violin, or Vini's iconoclastic virtuosity, and just the feel of the pieces, all transporting us to some high-ceilinged apartment in Brussels or Didsbury with the hum of hash in the air. For Manchester old-timers, Balearic types and dream pop lovers, this record is hugely recommended.

items.body:
Foreshadowing the later rush of shoegaze-inspired ambient music and joining the dots between MBV and Flying Saucer Attack and later experimentally-minded innovators like Fennesz and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, Midwestern duo loveliescrushing created something enduringly euphoric and shockingly prophetic on their 1993 debut album..

It's hard to believe this one came quite so early. The ingredients were there, sure: Spacemen 3's druggy, phased feedback; Kevin Shields' master-tape warping sonic maximalism; Glenn Branca's symphonic, detuned repetitions; Robin Guthrie's chorus-drenched strums; and Brian Eno's heady long-form muzak. But nobody had spotted the connections before - it took a duo far removed from the inward-looking Thames Valley scene to unhook shoegaze's textures from its song structures. So, a year before Dave Pierce masterminded "rural psychedelia" on 'Flying Saucer Attack', multi instrumentalist and producer Scott Cortez and vocalist Melissa Arpin-Duimstra released 'Bloweyelashwish', a noisy collage of blown-out tape loops, brickwall distortions and angelic chorals that'd be remixed and repackaged for a Projekt Records reissue in 1994. 

This latest reissue from Numero has been remastered and bulked out with five additional archival discoveries, bundled with lyrics and a postcard for good measure. And although loveliescrushing would perfect the formula on 1996's heartbreaking 'Xuvetyn' before going on hiatus, their debut has aged like wine, its Portastudio grit reminding us exactly what's missing from the barrage of horizontal, faintly nostalgic ambient-noise albums released each Friday. Cortez and Arpin-Duimstra were genuinely peering into the future with this one. Think of it as a concrète precursor to Fennesz's laptop-damaged 2001 classic 'Endless Summer'.

items.body:
Imagination's 1983 album 'Night Dubbing' re-issued on WRWTFWW.

"Night Dubbing is a refined deconstruction of black British soul and club pop, filtered through the deep studio and mixing techniques of dub music. Elegant, restrained, and, in its very own subtle way, radical, the record reshapes choice selections from the group’s stellar catalogue into an immersive and otherworldly experience.

The special mixes on Night Dubbing are built on time and space. Basslines elongate and dissolve. Vocals appear, vanish, and reappear like ghosts. Drums fall away into vast silences, while echoes, tape edits, and precise engineering manoeuvres smoothly slide across the stereo field, revealing themselves like magic over repeated listens. Far from simple extensions or 12” versions, Night Dubbing treats the studio itself as an instrument, opening new dimensions of sound. Often cited as a foundational record in the genesis of the house genre, the album also features the historic Larry Levan remix of "Changes", a Paradise Garage anthem that helped shape the direction of club music for decades to come."

More than 40 years on, Night Dubbing remains a seminal work. Its influence continues to echo through contemporary dance music, offering a blueprint for how pop could be transformed into something darker, stranger, more physical - a timeless sound that drifts effortlessly from the dancefloor into space.

New LP from Leipzig's tibslc via Glasgow's co:clear.

"co:clear is blessed to share the latest offering of Leipzig-based artist, tibslc. Like many, we were introduced to her work through those two stunner long-players on Sferic at the turn of the decade. In the here and now, we are pleased to showcase ‘City of Something’ – 8 fragments of deluxe hi-fi ambient that further dissolves us in digital haze. Traversing through meticulous fragments of sound, tiblsc entices the listener to her synthetic dreamworld with an album of deep, euphonic electronics. Serene moments of singer-songwriting are sprinkled throughout and remind us of the artist’s delicate ability to captivate with her ethereal voice.

Artwork comes courtesy of Berlin-based artist, Margarita Maximova."

items.body:
Pure charver archaeology: 1 hour of Mackem Makina importer, DJ Scott marshalling the Rockport and Air Max stompers at Hangar 13 v Uprising, May 2004. Fucking well aye mush!!!

As the story goes, DJ Scott was the first to bring the bouncy sound of Valencia queer megaclubs to England’s ultra macho working class North East, where, after a while, and the addition of MCs, it took root as local phenomenon; effectively a form of contemporary folk dance that mostly exists on the A19 leyline which joins Doncaster to Sunderland’s New Monkey club, but spiritually extends to Scotland, with an A66 spur to Redcar’s Powerhouse.

Long looked down on by snobs, the key working class sound of the NE has been rehabilitated and reclaimed in recent years to varying levels of ironic distance by London LARPers and expressly queer kids who would not have had a great time in the OG clubs in the early ‘00s, but can now enjoy the sound in their own spaces without fear of getting casually glassed or flegged-on. This tape looks back to that era when Makina, or Monta Musica, as it became known, was most often played at underage clubs - The New Monkey, or Hangar 13 - which only sold water and pop at the bar, but everyone was clearly tanning loads of wizz and pills. Depending on one’s proximity to Makina’s NE and Scottish stomping grounds, it’ll be either heaven or hell, but either way it’s 100% radge.

Prolific Canadians Priori & Project Pablo, aka Jump Source, refract fine strains of deep house, indie-pop, dub and techno-pop on an expansive LP ft. guest vox by billy woods, CFCF & Loukeman and advised to admirers of Luomo, Nick Léon, Rosa Terenzi & D. Tiffany, Galcher Lustwerk.

Building on a decade of Jump Source 12”s for Pacific Rhythm and their self-titled label, Francis Latreille & Patrick Holland skip to the former’s mothership, NAFF, for the project’s variegated debut album. The range and subtle recombinant steez of ‘Fold’ plays deep into the duo’s role at the core of Canada’s renowned club sound, which has emerged over the past decade with canniest updates and refinements of ‘90s to ‘00s US, UK x EU house, techno, trance and beyond. All the above can be heard stripped for parts and reassembled according to classic club lust and galvanised with slick production sure to see it gather air miles.

Tune to tune they fine-tune nuanced aspects of style and pattern, from tweaked darkroom electro-house with over-the-shoulder vox in ‘Nice & Edgy’ calling to mind Cheap & Deep Productions, to the pearlescent ambient-pop of ‘Close’ ft. POiSON GiRL FRiEND. Standouts are registered in the deep house of ‘Empty Bars’ that finds cult rapper billy woods out of context on a groove co-produced with Nick Léon, and in the echoes of Canadian click-house pioneer Akufen on ‘Affect’ ft. Loukeman, thru the brisker deep techno-house of ‘Fade City’ ft. Deaton Chris Anthony, and the Luomo-esque, connoisseurs choice of ‘A Dull Knife’ faced by Harmony Index.

Part 1 of a 12" series featuring Beatrice M.’s 'Sinking', the rudely aerodynamic debut LP where Tectonic's franco-british hope flexes a signature balance of ruff & smooth, building on a solid reputation earned via 12”s with her label, Bait, plus Tempa and Darwin’s SPE:C.​

Dubstep is not necessarily an album genre: beyond scant examples from the likes of Burial, Shackleton, or 2562, 12”s and DJ sets serve the sound in best context. However, Beatrice M.’s grasp of subtle sensuality and propulsive traction patently ends itself well to the format on ’Sinking’, with rolling, stepping and skanking permutations that deftly dance in the space between dubstep, proper, and its close-related cousins - UKG, broken beat, dub techno - with a finely measured proprioception of space, weight and pressure. 

Along with 2562’s recently dispensed ‘Lost Dubs 2006-09’, ’Sinking’ is arguably the best thing on Tectonic in recent memory, with a sound that revels in more ambiguous club suss. It’s the type of release primed for cans/buds as much as big cones, proving she’s equally adept at sublime tension, as in the languid ‘Ever’, as propelling a dance in the Martyn-esque wriggler ‘Motion’, and offbeat hood of ‘Disco Corner’.

Echospace Detroit’s Stephen Hitchell is at his most romantic, club-friendly and elemental on these effortless dub house glyders, newly remastered by Pole for posterity and optimal immersion

Originally issued on 12” in 2015 and hard-to-find ever since, ‘Lost Sequence’ is classic, archetypal Echospace tackle. The OG goes for 14 mins of strutting deep house groove swaddled in velvet-coated textures dubbed to the rafters and happy to hold its lane for the duration, adding extra layers of conga and crackling atmosphere as it proceeds. Hitchell’s Intrusion dub pitches the same elements in a spring weather system, drenching everything in fine mist of elemental FX and loosening the bass drum to a satisfyingly soggy slosh for 16 minutes of hypnotic bliss out.
